content: Smallpox is a highly contagious disease that exclusively affects humans. It is caused by two variants of the variola virus: Variola major and Variola minor. Variola major is the more severe form, with a mortality rate of 30–35%, while Variola minor causes a milder illness known as alastrim, which has a fatality rate of approximately 1%. Survivors of smallpox often bear permanent skin scars, and some may experience complications such as blindness due to corneal ulcerations or infertility in male patients. Smallpox has profoundly influenced human history and is believed to have existed for at least 16,000 years. The earliest clinical evidence of the disease was identified in the mummified remains of the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramses V. Smallpox has also been weaponized throughout history, with one of the most recent examples being its use during World War II. Following extensive vaccination campaigns in the 19th and 20th centuries, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, making it the first human infectious disease to be completely eliminated. The eradication of smallpox required a coordinated global effort, as the disease posed a universal threat. The process was both time-consuming and costly. After the last known death from a smallpox-related laboratory accident in 1978, all remaining stocks of the virus were destroyed, except for those retained for research purposes at the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Russian State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology (VECTOR). The variola virus is transmitted through contaminated surfaces or aerosolized particles. It evades the host's immune system and replicates within host cells, causing three clinical forms of the disease: ordinary smallpox, flat-type smallpox, and hemorrhagic smallpox. The virus is known for its characteristic skin lesions and has a unique ability to replicate in the cytoplasm of host cells, unlike most other DNA viruses. Humans are the only known host species for the variola virus, and its transmission occurs primarily through respiratory droplets. Before its eradication, smallpox needed to be distinguished from other diseases that cause vesicular rashes and fever, such as chickenpox, herpes zoster, and erythema multiforme. The true incidence of smallpox prior to eradication is difficult to determine due to underreporting, particularly in endemic regions. Children and young adults were the most affected demographic, especially in areas with low immunity levels. There was no evidence of gender or racial differences in disease incidence, but developing countries experienced higher rates of infection. In the modern era, individuals working in laboratories with the virus or those in areas targeted by bioterrorism are at potential risk. The clinical course of smallpox typically begins with flu-like symptoms, followed by the appearance of a skin rash that progresses to scabs, which eventually fall off, leaving scars. Complications can include respiratory conditions such as bronchitis or pneumonia, as well as joint, bone, or ocular involvement. The overall fatality rate for Variola major was approximately 30%. The diagnosis of smallpox was guided by a CDC-developed algorithm based on major and minor criteria. Common symptoms included high fever, malaise, fatigue, muscle pain, vomiting, and a rash that initially appeared in the oral mucosa before spreading to the skin. Physical examination findings varied depending on the disease stage and could include fever, tachycardia, skin and mucosal rashes, abdominal pain, ophthalmological changes, and altered mental status. Laboratory confirmation involved polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing or viral growth in specialized cell cultures. There is no specific antiviral treatment for smallpox. Management focuses on supportive care, including hydration, fever and pain control, and treatment of secondary bacterial or viral infections. In the absence of an outbreak, the vaccine is reserved for laboratory and clinical personnel working with the virus. However, the vaccine has notable adverse effects, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals or those with pre-existing heart conditions or allergies, necessitating careful administration. The CDC has developed protocols to protect the population in the event of a smallpox outbreak. The eradication of smallpox was a cost-effective public health achievement, as the disease was successfully eliminated. Despite its eradication, research continues to develop antiviral therapies for smallpox due to concerns about potential outbreaks or its use as a bioterrorism agent.
